walkthrough:
Seeing maternal-only transmission**
Think of mitochondria as tiny batteries in the cytoplasm that come only from the mother, because the egg provides the cytoplasm and the sperm provides almost none. That means if the mutation is in mtDNA, every child of an affected mother should get it, but no child of an affected father should get it from him.

Matching the pedigree to mtDNA**
Look at affected female 4 crossed with unaffected male 3. All three children 8, 9 and 10 are affected. Look at affected female 10 crossed with unaffected male 11. Both children 19 and 20 are affected. Now look at affected male 5 crossed with unaffected female 6. All three children 13, 14 and 15 are unaffected. Affected male 8 crossed with unaffected female 7 also gives unaffected children 17 and 18. Fathers never pass it on, mothers pass it to all children. That is exactly maternal mtDNA inheritance.

Why it cannot be X-linked**
An X chromosome gene behaves very differently. A male has only one X, inherited from his mother, so a single faulty allele on that X will show up. This usually makes X-linked conditions more common in males and produces carrier females who carry the allele but look unaffected. Here the opposite is seen: more females are affected than males, and every female is either clearly affected or clearly unaffected with no carriers.

Putting the evidence together**
State both sides clearly with numbers: mtDNA is supported because transmission is only through affected females to all their children, and X-linkage is ruled out because males do not show the expected higher frequency and no heterozygous carrier females exist.

Final answer: Maternal mtDNA inheritance: affected males do not pass MELAS to any offspring, e.g. 5 x 6 gives unaffected 13, 14, 15 and 8 x 7 gives unaffected 17, 18; all children of affected females inherit MELAS, e.g. 4 gives affected 8, 9, 10 and 10 gives affected 19, 20. Not X-linked as more females than males are affected and there are no unaffected carrier females, whereas X-linked traits affect males more because males have only one X chromosome.

hints: Think about what evolution studies need - a way to measure how long ago two species split apart by counting differences in DNA. What kind of mutation pattern would act like a clock?
Compare mitochondrial and nuclear DNA packaging, but do not assume mitochondria lack repair enzymes. The historical scheme includes that obsolete simplification; use the other supported comparisons.
Think about what happens to nuclear DNA at fertilisation and meiosis - mixing from two parents and crossing over - and why mtDNA avoids this because it comes from only one parent.
walkthrough:
mtDNA as a molecular clock**
To tell how recently species diverged you count differences in the same gene. mtDNA is ideal because mutations build up at a fairly constant rate, and faster than in nuclear DNA. More differences means a longer time since the common ancestor, fewer differences means a more recent split.

Interpret the historical comparison carefully**
Mitochondrial DNA does not have the same histone packaging as nuclear chromosomes, but mitochondria do possess DNA-repair mechanisms, including base-excision repair. The historical mark scheme states that mtDNA lacks repair enzymes; that statement is an obsolete simplification and should not be used as a scientific explanation of its mutation rate.

Why the signal stays clean**
Nuclear DNA is shuffled every generation by getting one set from each parent and by crossing over, which mixes the story. mtDNA is circular, comes only from the mother, and has no crossing over. Any change you see must be a new mutation passed down that maternal line, making family trees much simpler to trace.

Final answer: Mutations in mtDNA occur at a constant and faster rate than in nuclear DNA; mtDNA does not have the same histone packaging as nuclear chromosomes; mtDNA is maternally inherited with no mixing at fertilisation and no crossing over, so all sequence differences are mutations; many copies per cell aid analysis. Scientific qualification: mitochondria have DNA-repair mechanisms; the historical repair-enzyme criterion is retained only in the original mark scheme.
